data.title: Set up a machine and project from one pasted link
Decide whether to push agents-md and move the 33% limit everywhere
data.description:
New users get `agents-md` from GitHub, so the `harness` default and the 33% limit don't reach them until it's pushed. `main` is two commits ahead: 22b9a51 (Ben's, raises the limit to 33%) and b6e1a33 (adds `harness`). The repo is public, so pushing needs Ben's OK. His uncommitted `modules/design-process.md` edit stays out of it.

After the push, run `agents update` in this repo, which is still pinned to 99458a4 and renders 25%. `contextfill`'s README and OpenCode plugin both still say `--main-max 25`, and so does Ben's own global hook, which is his to change.

Out of scope: rolling the new pin across Ben's other repos.

criteria.label: Ben has ruled on the push and any push is done
This repo renders 33% after agents update
The contextfill README and plugin say --main-max 33, or a note says why not

data.title: Find out what agents init and job init do to an existing project
data.description:
The setup has to be safe in a project that already has files, and `SETUP.md` should be written from what these tools actually do. The `agents init` help says existing `AGENTS.md` content becomes the project-owned head and that it links `CLAUDE.md`. No one has yet checked a real `CLAUDE.md` file with no `AGENTS.md`, or a symlink, an existing `.gitignore`, a folder that isn't a Git repo, or a second run.

Try each case in a scratch folder, with `AGENTS_REGISTRY` and `AGENTS_CACHE` pointed at scratch so Ben's real registry stays clean. Fix a tool bug at its source, or file it, rather than working around it in the playbook.

Where the answer goes: a dated findings doc under `project/`.

criteria.label: A findings doc lists each case, the command run and the outcome
Any case that loses user content is fixed or has a job filed against it

data.title: Ship the Go tools as signed bottles
data.description:
`job` and `agents` only install with `go install`, and `contextfill` builds from source, so a new user would need Go. Add formulae for `job` and `agents` to `homebrew-tap`, and set `bottle=yes`, `sign=` and `notary_profile=` in each tool's `scripts/release.conf`, following `woodcase`'s. Each tool releases itself with `homebrew-tap`'s `scripts/release`.

Check each repo is public first; `gh` was blocked in the sandbox when this plan was written. Releases push tags and upload bottles, so they need Ben's OK and his signing credentials. Update each README's install section to lead with `brew install bensyverson/tap/<tool>`.

Risk: bottles are tagged for the formula's oldest macOS, and the binary must target that release.

criteria.label: brew install of job, agents and contextfill pours a bottle with no Go installed, shown on a clean account
codesign and spctl checks pass on each binary

data.title: Ship sleepy and peep as signed bottles
data.description:
Neither tool is in the tap: `sleepy` (repo `sleepyhollow`) and `peep` (repo `PixelPeeper`) install from source today. Add formulae and bottles the same way `woodcase` does, including any resource bundle that has to sit beside the binary.

Two traps. `sleepy`'s `Package.swift` deliberately pins the macOS 12 SDK at link time because WebKit gates behavior on it, so a build that loses that flag can pass and still behave wrongly. `PixelPeeper` has no LICENSE file, and Ben needs to confirm one before it ships publicly.

Same release constraints as the Go tools: Ben's OK and his signing credentials.

criteria.label: brew install of sleepy and peep pours a bottle without Xcode, shown on a clean account
otool -l on the bottled sleepy shows the same SDK version as a source build
PixelPeeper has a LICENSE

data.title: Write the README, SETUP.md and Brewfile
data.description:
This is the product. The plan doc's "How the link works" and "Setup order" sections hold the agreed flow, including the Homebrew, `gh` and `PATH` steps, and its "Decisions" section binds this leaf.

Write for someone who may never have used a terminal: explain each tool in a sentence or two. Keep the README tight and put the steps in `SETUP.md`. A fetch tool may summarize long pages, so tell the agent to read the raw file and say how. Each step checks before it acts, so a second run changes nothing. Include a short section per tool for Claude Code and OpenCode, and document what OpenCode lacks: `harness.md` only covers Claude Code.

`SETUP.md` also creates `local/` and explains it, because that rule lives here. Installing the tools depends on the bottle leaves for real use, but the text can be written before they ship.

criteria.label: The README opens with what this is and what changes, and points agents at SETUP.md
SETUP.md covers every step in the plan, including declining Homebrew and declining gh
A dry read in a fresh session finds no step that needs this planning conversation

data.title: Ship the machine-wide settings
data.description:
Two Claude Code settings are recommended, each offered with consent: the `contextfill` hook (`--max 40 --main-max 33`) and the plan-mode block. Ben's block lives at `~/.claude/hooks/block-plan-mode.sh`, outside any repo, and it needs `jq`. Decide where the script ships from and add `jq` if it stays a dependency. It only denies plan mode in folders with a `.jobs.db`, so it's safe to install globally.

The setup must merge into an existing `settings.json`, never overwrite it. OpenCode gets the `contextfill` plugin link from the formula's caveats.

criteria.label: Running the step on an existing settings.json keeps every existing key, shown by a before and after diff
A second run adds nothing
The hook reports fill in a live session on a clean account

data.title: Decide whether the setup recommends the Bash sandbox
data.description: `harness.md` assumes the Bash sandbox is on, so a new user without it reads rules about failures they won't see. Options: recommend it as a third setting, or leave it off and reword `harness.md`. Ben's question to answer; the settings and playbook leaves wait on it only for one paragraph.

data.title: Decide whether to remove Ben-specific wording from the modules
data.description: Some shared rules assume Ben's machine: `web.md` says `sleepy` is "on this machine". Rewording reaches all his repos on their next update, and the question is still open with Ben.

data.title: Run the whole setup on a clean Mac
data.description:
This is the plan's definition of done. Ben's own Mac already has everything installed, so only a new macOS account or VM counts, starting without Homebrew or the Command Line Tools. Paste the repo URL with no other words into fresh Claude Code and OpenCode sessions, once in an empty folder and once in an existing project, then run it a second time.

Needs Ben or another person at the keyboard for the terminal steps.

criteria.label: An empty folder and an existing project both finish with a clean agents check and a working job orient, in Claude Code
The same two runs finish in OpenCode, with any gaps matching what SETUP.md documents
A second run changes nothing, shown by git status
Declining Homebrew leaves the folder untouched
Findings are recorded in a dated doc under project/

data.new_desc:
This is the plan's definition of done. Ben's test: someone boots a brand-new MacBook Neo for the first time, installs Claude Code, and pastes the repo URL into the thread. Do they get up and running, and do they learn what is being installed and why?

Use a real MacBook Neo if possible, otherwise a new macOS account or VM with no Homebrew or Command Line Tools, and record which one it was, because a new account on Ben's Mac doesn't fully prove a new machine. Paste the URL with no other words into a fresh Claude Code session, starting in the default folder, then repeat in an existing project and run a second time. Then repeat in OpenCode.

Have a person who doesn't know these tools read the transcript, or ask them afterward, because the teaching can't be checked by a script.

Needs a person at the keyboard for the terminal steps.

criteria.label: From a brand-new Mac with only Claude Code installed, a pasted URL alone reaches a clean agents check and a working job orient
Started in the home folder, setup creates a project folder and leaves the home folder uninitialized
Before each install the transcript says what the tool is and why, and a reader new to these tools can explain them afterward

data.text: Ben's test now binds this leaf: a brand-new MacBook Neo with only Claude Code installed, and the user may never have used a terminal. Before each install, say what the tool is and why. New steps are in the plan doc: don't initialize the home folder, and check `xcode-select -p` rather than `command -v git`, because /usr/bin/git is a stub until the Command Line Tools are installed. Confirm the repo and raw file URLs load without any sign-in, since a new user has no gh.

data.note: Ben ruled 2026-11-05: leave the sandbox off by default. harness.md should say its sandbox failures only apply when it's on. The rewording itself rides with the wording leaf (DhuGEt).

data.text: Ben ruled 2026-11-05: yes, make the modules universal. This includes saying in harness.md that the sandbox section only applies when the sandbox is on. Not started; Ben asked to stay in planning first.

data.text: Ben ruled 2026-11-05 that contextfill stays pure, so there is no config file, built-in limit or advice text. What's left: change README and OpenCode plugin from --main-max 25 to 33, and optionally "(over 33%)" to "(past 33%)". data.title: Build the local setup page and its one source of tool facts
data.description:
Everything a new user reads comes from here, so write this first. The plan's "The interface" section holds the rulings: a local page served by a short script on the system Perl (HTTP::Daemon), bound to 127.0.0.1 with a random token, downloaded with curl and read by the agent before it runs. Fast path and guided path, toggles for skippable tools, live progress. There's no hosted page: if the script can't run, the agent says so and continues in the chat.

One file holds what each tool is, why it's there, whether it can be skipped and which modules recommend it. The page and agent both read it. The plan's "Required and skippable tools" section has the split.

Evidence: project/2026-11-05-stock-macos-runtimes.md. Risk: Apple may remove the system Perl, so the chat path must stay complete, not a degraded afterthought. Follow the Previews principle: the page needs a way to render in each state without running a setup.

criteria.label: On a Mac with no developer tools, the page opens and the agent receives the choices, shown on the clean-Mac run
With the script unavailable, the same setup finishes in the chat with the same facts
A request without the token is refused, shown by a test

data.title: Add pro mode and a new-project shortcut
data.description:
Ben will use this himself to set up new project folders, so it must be quick for someone who already knows it. The first run offers "skip the tour next time" and saves that in bootstrap's own preferences file, not in any tool's. After that: no browser, no explanations, only questions the agent can't detect, and a short summary. Steps already done skip themselves, so a set-up Mac only meets the project part.

Also offer to install a `/new-project` command that fetches the latest SETUP.md. Check what the OpenCode equivalent is. Open: exact preferences location, and whether to remember answers like the usual stage.

criteria.label: On a Mac already set up, with the preference on, a new folder is ready with no browser and only undetectable questions

data.title: Offer /remote-control as the last setup step
data.description: Ben recommends beginners drive Claude Code with /remote-control from the web or app. Offer it as the last step, because the Homebrew install needs someone at the Mac. Find out which accounts and plans can use it, and what it needs on a new Mac, then write the step. Skipping must be fine.

criteria.label: SETUP.md states who can use it, with the source, and the step works on the clean-Mac run

data.text: Ben's visual brief and first mock are in the plan's "The interface" section and project/2026-11-05-setup-page-mock/setup.pen. The mock fakes the object with blurred gradients; the morphing has to be proven in Three.js. Open: Perl script or a signed, notarized binary as the server.

Motion prototype built outside the repo, with Grand embedded: fast while working, slow while waiting. Glass is metaballs from a raymarched shader; threads are GPU line ribbons. Checked in headless WebKit: both render, no console errors, no overflow at 400px. Headless frames don't tick, so live motion and frame rate are unchecked.

data.new_title: Build the bootstrap Go binary and its page
data.old_desc:
Everything a new user reads comes from here, so write this first. The plan's "The interface" section holds the rulings: a local page served by a short script on the system Perl (HTTP::Daemon), bound to 127.0.0.1 with a random token, downloaded with curl and read by the agent before it runs. Fast path and guided path, toggles for skippable tools, live progress. There's no hosted page: if the script can't run, the agent says so and continues in the chat.

One file holds what each tool is, why it's there, whether it can be skipped and which modules recommend it. The page and agent both read it. The plan's "Required and skippable tools" section has the split.

Evidence: project/2026-11-05-stock-macos-runtimes.md. Risk: Apple may remove the system Perl, so the chat path must stay complete, not a degraded afterthought. Follow the Previews principle: the page needs a way to render in each state without running a setup.
data.new_desc:
This is what a new user sees and reads. It turns the approved prototype into a real signed program, so an agent can show progress and collect choices on a Mac that may have nothing installed.

**What exists when it's done:** a Go program, `bootstrap`, with a library core and a thin CLI. It serves the page on 127.0.0.1 and gives the agent a small JSON command line along the lines of detect, serve, step and wait. The agent still does the installing. All screens and copy live in the binary, so an agent can't invent wording, and the launching agent's name comes from a flag.

**Already decided (Ben, 2026-11-05):** Go, signed and notarized. Threads, in linear light. No hard cuts: every change animates, and what leaves and what arrives share one 1.4s S-curve. The object never moves. See "The interface" in project/2026-11-05-setup-link-plan.md. The prototype in project/2026-11-05-setup-page-mock/prototype/ is the visual reference, including its timing constants and shaders. Its bottom study bar, fake waits and "I did it" buttons are not part of the product.

**Seams:** new Go module in this repo. Embed the page, Three.js (no CDN), the subset Grand fonts and the card images. One shared struct for events across the CLI and the page.

**Security:** bind to loopback, require a random token, check Host and Origin, exit after the agent stops sending heartbeats. Test each refusal.

**Open:** real data for the Homebrew and Git cards, which are made up in the prototype. Long steps may only be able to show elapsed time. The agent's call on the exact verbs.

**Risks:** the float buffer costs more to draw on weak Macs, so keep an eight-bit path. An agent may hesitate to run a downloaded binary, tested in its own leaf.

data.title: Test the risky assumptions on the Mini, a VM and the Air
data.description:
Decides whether the plan holds before the rest gets built around it. Ben can't wipe or buy a Mac, so project/2026-11-05-clean-mac-research.md splits the testing across machines.

**Questions:** Will an agent, given only the pasted link, verify and run a signed binary, and in Claude Code and OpenCode alike? Does xcode-select --install, then Homebrew, then the tools work from nothing in a clean VM? Can the file /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/bin/git be polled to detect the end of Apple's install? Do the threads run smoothly on the MacBook Air?

**Where:** the agent trial on the Mac Mini in a new folder; the first-run flow in a Tart vanilla VM on the Mini (first check it really lacks the tools); the graphics check by opening local.html on the Air, with its owner's OK and nothing installed. Ben has to be at the machines, or give access.

**If an agent refuses the binary:** consider a script bootstrap, a clearer SETUP.md, or starting in chat. Record which.

criteria.label: A dated findings doc records each question, the machine, the command and what happened
An agent's response to the pasted link is recorded for Claude Code and OpenCode
The first-run flow is recorded from a VM confirmed to have no Command Line Tools

data.text: Correction: check for /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/bin/git rather than xcode-select -p, as Homebrew does. See project/2026-11-05-clean-mac-research.md. Fonts, Three.js and the page now ship inside the bootstrap binary. Homebrew can install the tools itself without Apple's window, which is an open choice for Ben.
